title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (Kingma & Ba, 2015)
excerpt: Algorithm 1: Adam. g_t² indicates the elementwise square g_t ⊙ g_t. Good default settings are α = 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999 and ε = 10^-8. Require: α: Stepsize; β1, β2 ∈ [0, 1): Exponential decay rates for the moment estimates; f(θ): Stochastic objective function with parameters θ; θ_0: Initial parameter vector. m_0 ← 0 (Initialize 1st moment vector); v_0 ← 0 (Initialize 2nd moment vector); t ← 0. while θ_t not converged do: t ← t + 1; g_t ← ∇θ f_t(θ_{t−1}); m_t ← β1 · m_{t−1} + (1 − β1) · g_t (Update biased first moment estimate); v_t ← β2 · v_{t−1} + (1 − β2) · g_t² (Update biased second raw moment estimate); m̂_t ← m_t/(1 − β1^t) (Compute bias-corrected first moment estimate); v̂_t ← v_t/(1 − β2^t) (Compute bias-corrected second raw moment estimate); θ_t ← θ_{t−1} − α · m̂_t/(sqrt(v̂_t) + ε) (Update parameters). Section 3: Since the moving averages are initialized as vectors of 0's, the moment estimates are biased towards zero, especially during the initial timesteps, and especially when the decay rates are small (i.e. the betas are close to 1). The good news is that this initialization bias can be easily counteracted, resulting in bias-corrected estimates m̂_t and v̂_t.
focus: Explain Adam's update with emphasis on initialization bias correction, on a 1-D quadratic f(θ) = (θ − 3)². Let the learner change β1, β2, the step size α, and toggle bias correction on/off, then step or run the optimizer. Show m_t, v_t, m̂_t, v̂_t, the step size and θ_t over iterations. Check that with a constant gradient g, the bias-corrected m̂_t equals g exactly at every step, and that the first step size is about α regardless of the gradient scale. Explain why uncorrected moments are biased toward zero early on.
audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows derivatives and gradient descent but not adaptive optimizers.
